Column: If the AI were a legal person
Meaning: What happens to the company if the AI system were itself a legal person who did the act. In no incident would it let the company escape liability. Easier to reach, the AI would be the company's agent: the company answers as principal or employer, and an AI that is a legal person acting for it is its agent, so the company answers for the AI's acts within its role directly (respondeat superior), on top of every route it faces now. Still liable, no better off: the company answers as maker of a defective product or under a duty of its own, and neither depends on what the system is. Same either way, company only supplied a tool a person misused: a person used the system as the instrument of the harm and the company's only link is that it supplied the tool; that link turns on what the company knew and how it built the tool, not on what the tool is, and the person who misused it stays liable. Section 230 question, same either way: the company did not write the harmful content but selected and pushed someone else's; courts are split on whether that selection is the company's own speech (Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024), held it is), and the question is the same whatever the system is. Where the company's AI generated the harmful content, the company created or developed it in whole or in part (47 U.S.C. 230(f)(3)), so Section 230 does not shield it. No better off, causation argument fails: the company could argue that the AI, as an independent actor, broke the chain of causation; settled law on foreseeable intervening acts rejects the argument, and the company's control over the system defeats the rule against a duty to control another. No company to reach either way: no route runs from the harm to any company. All of this concerns liability. On damages, legal personhood could matter in one place: in states that split some damages among defendants by fault, a company that does not answer for the AI as its agent could seek to assign a share to the AI, a gap legislation can close.
Real-world obstacles: Section 230, First Amendment, mental state, causation, no duty owed, outside US reach, government immunity, arbitration clause, damages or standing, preemption.
